subject: 79B6F204399AE4F22739206947ECBC2A
introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá lived into the age of the camera, and people wanted his photograph. He gave it, sometimes reluctantly, and laid down a rule that Bahá’ís still keep: a portrait may be kept with respect as a remembrance, but is not to be hung up or made an object of devotion; the photograph of Bahá’u’lláh is not displayed at all; and imaginary pictures of the Manifestations are not to be made. The second commandment and Deuteronomy’s “ye saw no manner of similitude” are the root of that caution; Paul and Barnabas tearing their clothes at Lystra show its motive; and “blessed are they that have not seen” is its consolation. Habakkuk’s scorn of images is set against the long experience of traditions that pray before them.
questions: What is the difference between a portrait kept as a remembrance and one kept as an object of devotion? Can the difference be seen from outside?
Why would the likeness of the Founder of a religion be withheld from display?
What do images of holy figures do for people, and what do they risk?

outside.why: A question about the picture of “this oppressed one”. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing.
A photograph sent to a distant friend. Whom having not seen, ye love.
He went to the studio twice, for a friend’s sake. Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Against imaginary portraits of holy figures. He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.

Is this the time for plays about the Faith’s history? At Lystra the crowd cried, the gods are come down to us in the likeness of men; and the apostles rent their clothes: we also are men of like passions with you.
Place the Greatest Name in your dwelling: a word, where others hang a picture. These words shall be in thine heart, and thou shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house.
The photograph is not to be hung in rooms. Ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the Lord spake unto you: lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image.
Friends asking for a likeness. Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.

The people of doubt have created an imaginary portrait. Habakkuk’s whole judgment on images: what profiteth the graven image? Christians and Hindus have prayed before images for centuries and found them a help. What do the readings fear from a portrait, and what do they allow it?
Photographs of historic places requested. That ye may look upon it, and remember.
A closing reply on the same matter. Now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
